prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms enabled frequency standards at the 1e-18 level.

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B006 to B015. In round 1 my objection was that the lattice clock is an enabling instrument rather than a discovery about nature, and I asked what it has taught us. The replies were more concrete than I expected: Katori's magic-wavelength idea is a real piece of atomic-structure physics, Ye's group resolved a gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample, and it had to master many-body and Fermi-degenerate effects to reach about 1e-18. Independent agreement at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL, and the route to constraints on constants and to the redefinition of the second, show that the claim is settled and used. The two-name credit follows the real division of labour, concept and performance, and needs no truncation. The citation can be kept distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes by naming the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice, which the comb made countable and the ion work did not provide.
statement.case_against: My earlier preference for B006 still reflects a real taste: prediction followed by an unexpected result is the sequence I value most, and B006 remains the larger new field. I did not change because it is wrong, but because the interpretation is not yet fixed: the pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated states are open, twist-angle and sample disorder limit comparison, and the credited triple omits Cao and colleagues and earlier moire theory. For B015 itself the weak points are overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, contributions from single-ion clocks and from Paris, PTB and NIST lattice groups outside Katori and Ye, and the pending redefinition of the second. I see these as framing and credit-boundary issues, not doubts about the science. The measurement is also a capability more than a new phenomenon, and I do not want the citation to claim fundamental discoveries that have not yet been made.

responses.point: Holds B015 as the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, notes that B006 is arguably the larger wave and asks for a principled reason to omit it, and raises a possible two-part prize pairing the clock with a condensed-matter candidate.
responses.response: The principled reason is maturity of interpretation, not size: B006 is larger, but the citation would have to be written around observation because the mechanism is unresolved. I do not think a two-part prize with B006 works on the numbers, since it would force at most one of the three laureates onto the second part and would break the real theory-plus-experiment triple. I would rather keep B006 whole for a later year than truncate it. On the SI second, I treat redefinition as supporting evidence and not a precondition; the clocks already operate and are compared internationally, so the discovery or invention does not depend on a metrological decision.

responses.point: Argues that Katori's magic wavelength is a real atomic-structure insight and that the lattice clock is a distinct step from the comb, because the comb makes optical frequencies countable and the lattice clock is what is counted. She also warns that a narrow citation may look as if it excludes the single-ion lineage.
responses.response: Your comb-versus-clock distinction is what moved me on the novelty question, and I would put it in the citation by naming the neutral-atom lattice and magic-wavelength trapping explicitly. On the ion-clock lineage, I think the answer is to word the citation narrowly and honestly rather than to widen the credit: the lattice architecture with thousands of atoms interrogated at once is what Katori and Ye contributed, and single-ion clocks reached comparable uncertainty by a different technique with a different credit story. I accept that a wider citation covering all optical clocks would reopen attribution toward Wineland's group and Paris and PTB, and I do not support that. I do not think your own proximity to the field disqualifies you; I would just ask that the discussion be tested against Kroll's reservations.

responses.point: Argues that B055 has the same prediction-plus-experiment structure with a stable interpretation, that B006's precursors (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto, Suarez Morell) make contested credit no advantage, and that B006 belongs in a later year.
responses.response: I accept the precursor point; it is fair, and it means I cannot claim B006 has the cleaner credit. I also agree that B055 is more settled than B006, which is why it remains my alternative along with B006. Where we still differ is B055's attribution: the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that told Molenkamp's group where to look and the Fu-Kane-Moore-Balents-Roy three-dimensional generalisation are outside the supplied names, and you list this yourself as the weak point. B015 has a cleaner credit and an experimental result confirmed to a quantitative standard, so I now rank it above B055, but I do not regard B055 as a poor case and would not oppose it if the committee found a framing that holds.

responses.point: Takes B006's originality seriously but does not want a citation that commits to an interpretation that might be retracted, flags the credit risk from the 2018 experimental team (Cao and colleagues), and says she would not obstruct B006 if the interpretation is judged settled.
responses.response: The citation worry is exactly right and it is part of why I moved: my round-1 wording named correlated insulating and superconducting states, which is about observation, but any version that went further would be premature. Your credit point about Cao and colleagues is one I had underweighted, because Jarillo-Herrero's name stands for a larger experimental team. I am glad to hear you would not obstruct B006, but I now agree with you that it is better held until the interpretation is clearer. Your request for a citation that separates the lattice clock from the frequency comb is one I share, and I would support wording the citation around magic-wavelength trapping and 1e-18 uncertainty.

responses.point: Considers B006 a credible near-future candidate but not the prize to be confident about now, since the lattice clock is stable and independently confirmed while the graphene interpretation may still move. Moved from B023 to B015 after the openings.
responses.response: I agree with your distinction between a result whose interpretation is stable and one that may still move, and it is the main reason I have followed you to B015. I differ on one point: I do not see a measurement capability as lesser, since the redshift across a millimetre and the many-body control were real physics, not just better precision. I also note that your own earlier preference, B023, had a credit gap on the exact-solution side, so we both accepted a cleaner configuration over a more attractive one. I still think the committee should say plainly in the citation that the lattice clock is a tool for tests of nature, not yet itself such a test, and I would keep the wording to what has been done.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the lattice-clock citation is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; I rely on recollection and have not verified detailed priority claims.

How much of the credit for the record uncertainties belongs to other lattice-clock groups (Paris, PTB, NIST, Ludlow and Lemke) and to the single-ion clock community, which I cannot check from the supplied material.

Whether B006 will be viewed as a missed opportunity if the correlated phases are better understood soon, and whether my change reflects a considered judgment on maturity or just the weight of other members' views; I have tried to base it on the physical evidence.
Whether the SI redefinition of the second should be treated as a precondition; I treat it as supporting and not decisive.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My documented connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, and none of them is among the credited names on B015, B006 or B055. I have no documented tie to Katori or Ye.
